sentences.text: The only known specimen of Ostromia is incomplete, preserving only limb bones, cervical vertebrae, and ribs.
Its hand structure shows a unique ratio between the third and first metacarpals compared to any Archaeopteryx specimen.
In this animal, the claw of the first hand digit is smaller than the corresponding metacarpal, whereas in Archaeopteryx the claw is larger.
The pubic bone of Ostromia is strongly flexed backwards with a triangular boot, a feature similar to Anchiornis but unlike Archaeopteryx.
The holotype specimen was discovered near Riedenburg, Germany, in 1855 and was originally misidentified as a pterosaur species named Pterodactylus crassipes in 1857.
In 1970, paleontologist John Ostrom identified the specimen as Archaeopteryx and named it the "Haarlem specimen" because it was housed in the Teylers Museum in Haarlem.
Ostromia fossils were recovered from the Late Jurassic Painten Formation in Germany and the genus was named by Christian Foth and Oliver Rauhut in 2017.
In 2017, Christian Foth and Oliver Rauhut reclassified the specimen as a new genus named Ostromia, honoring John Ostrom, after concluding it was more closely related to Anchiornis.
Foth and Rauhut (2017) classified Ostromia within the family Anchiornithidae as the only known European member.
Ostromia is classified within the family Anchiornithidae.
Ostromia lived during the Late Jurassic, specifically the Kimmeridgian stage, in what is now Europe.
Agnolin et al. (2019) debated that Ostromia should be considered an indeterminate paravian rather than an anchiornithid, citing similarities to Unenlagiinae.
Recent studies, including work by Mulder et al. (2024), suggest that micro-CT analysis may provide a definitive solution to the ongoing debate over Ostromia's classification.

A 2026 study by O'Connor & Marugán-Lobón argued that the diagnostic characters of Ostromia are equivocal and the fossil likely represents Archaeopteryx, while a subsequent 2026 revision by Foth & Rauhut interpreted it as an indeterminate avialan.
